speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONCLUSION OF NEW INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 21 I advised the house that a delegation was being sent from Canada to take part in the United Nations wheat conference at Geneva. Included in the Canadian delegation were members of the advisory committee of the Canadian wheat board who are at the same time leaders of the principal farm organizations in western Canada.
The purpose of the conference was to negotiate a new international wheat agreement. I am pleased to state that the negotiations in Geneva have come to a fruitful conclusion. Subject to ratification by the governments concerned, a new three-year international wheat agreement will enter into effect next August. I am advised that the new wheat agreement was negotiated in an atmosphere of international good will and co-operation, and that it is broader in scope and content than the present agreement and will cover the major proportion of the international wheat trade.
The new agreement differs in important respects from the agreements negotiated in 1949, 1953 and 1956. These earlier agreements were based upon rights and obligations which had effect only when prices reached the internationally agreed maximum and minimum. In the new agreement each of the importing countries has committed itself to buy a specified percentage of its annual commercial imports from the exporting countries at prices within the agreed price range. If, however, prices should go to the maximum the exporters' obligations to supply at that price are limited to the average commercial purchases of the importing countries over a recent period of years.
The objectives of the new agreement have been significantly broadened, and provision has been made for a comprehensive annual review by the international wheat council of developments affecting world trade in wheat, including surplus disposals. A new price range has been negotiated. The present minimum price of $1.50 per bushel basis No.
66968-9-113
1 Manitoba northern in store Fort William/-Port Arthur has been maintained unchanged and will be continued during the next three years. The maximum price has been established at $1.90 per bushel for the same grade of wheat in the same position.
It is a matter of satisfaction to Canada, and I think to all countries interested in international co-operation in wheat, that the United Kingdom, subject to parliamentary approval in that country, is likely to join the new agreement. The return of the United Kingdom to the international wheat agreement will strengthen the agreement and increase its effectiveness and value.
The text of the agreement will be submitted for ratification at the present session, and I trust it will commend itself to this house and to Canadian wheat producers.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONCLUSION OF NEW INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT

Mr. Speaker, we in this group over the years have supported the international wheat agreements which have been formulated from time to time. We are again pleased on this occasion to support the passage of this agreement and Canada's signature to it. The past agreement has really been quite ineffective because neither the ceiling price nor the floor price came into effect.
I think to appreciate the probable value of this agreement one must bear in mind that the ceiling price for No. 1 northern wheat at Fort William/Port Arthur today is in the neighbourhood of $1.70 a bushel, which means there is a 20 cent leeway in

The agreement itself is satisfactory, but I suggest it must be supplemented and supported by a program of deficiency payments to bolster our western farm incomes. speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: STATEMENT ON SALE OF OIL AND GAS PERMIT RIGHTS IN NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Hon. members will be pleased to hear that a public sale of oil and gas permit rights was held yesterday afternoon for 3,546,829 acres. All the acreage, except for some 250,000 acres, lies in the southwestern Northwest Territories and southeastern Yukon in the general vicinity of Fort Liard. Some 250 bids indicate the largest public interest in any sale ever held by the department, and also indicate that major exploration for oil and gas is moving northward into the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory.
Cash bonus bids to the value of over $6,500,000 will be accepted with some of the bids reaching nearly $9 per acre. This is all direct revenue to the crown. The successful bidders must spend $3 per acre over the nine

year term of each permit, which will amount to over $8,500,000 in actual exploration for oil and gas.
I should emphasize that this sale is for exploratory privileges only, though if the permittee complies with the regulations he may acquire up to 50 per cent of each area as an oil and gas lease. He must apply for such a lease if he discovers oil and gas and wishes to commence production.
I plan to make a full statement to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters on government policy regarding oil and gas and other minerals in northern Canada, and how the public interest is protected in the development of these resources.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister comment on a report in the New York Times of March 8 that the United States and Canada have agreed in principle on joint control of nuclear weapons and stockpiles of warheads to be based in Canada, and that an announcement on this matter is to be made shortly which would, among other things, state that such stockpiles in Canada would be under the direct control of United States personnel, as provided by United States law?
Righl Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I noticed that article; and while the hon. gentleman did not give me notice of his question I have made inquiries with regard to this matter and I find that the article appearing in the New York Times is inaccurate in a number of details.
The government does not anticipate concluding a formal agreement with the United States government on the acquisition of nuclear warheads in the immediate future. I would draw the attention of the house to the statement I made in this regard on February 20. I indicated then that it would be some time before nuclear weapons would and indeed could be available for use by Canadian forces. At that time I stated that as soon as the government was in a position to do so it would inform the house, within the limits of security, of the general terms of understanding reached between the two governments on this subject. I believe that is about as far as I can go on this occasion.

speechtext:
That the report of the Canada Council for the year ended March 31, 1958 laid before the house on July 10, 1958 be referred to the standing committee on public accounts in order to provide a review thereof pursuant to section 23 of the Canada Council Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to make any statement at this time except to point out that under the statute, chapter 3 of 1956-57, section 22 and section 23 read as follows:
22.	The accounts and financial transactions of the council shall be audited annually by the Auditor General, and a report of the audit shall be made to the council and to the member of the Queen's privy council for Canada designated under section 23.
23.	The chairman of the council shall, within three months after the termination of each fiscal year, submit to the member of the Queen's privy council for Canada designated by the governor in council for the purpose a report of all proceedings under this act for that fiscal year, including the financial statements of the council, and the Auditor General's report thereon, and the member so designated shall cause such reports to be laid before parliament within fifteen days after the receipt thereof or, if parliament is not then sitting, on any of the first fifteen days next thereafter that parliament is sitting and provision shall be made for a review thereof by parliament.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra suggested at the time this legislation was introduced that there should be some control by parliament over the expenditures of the Canada council, and it is pursuant to this that the section was accepted at the time. My understanding is that if this motion is acceptable a committee of this house will be set up, and in the other place the action taken will be to submit a report to the finance committee. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) referred to this matter on one occasion. I think it is generally agreed that an examination would be beneficial not only to the council itself but also to hon. members of this house.

[Mr. Fulton.)

subtopic: MOTION TO REFER CANADA COUNCIL REPORT TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very much in favour of this motion. One of the questions which comes to mind is whether it would not have been better to have left this until later in the session so that the more recent report might be before the committee. I suppose it could be argued that a year's interval since the last report would enable us to look at this subject in better perspective. But I think there have been many press releases made by the council since the time of the last report, and it seems to me that the council's activities are moving at such a speed and on such broad lines that we should try to keep up with them. It seems to me that we have a special responsibility so far as the Canada Council is concerned. I should like to make one of my points by reading from a report criticizing the council which was written by Richard Jackson of the Ottawa bureau of the Sudbury Star. The article is headed: "Culture Vultures may 'get lumps' " and it says, in part:
The Canada Council and the $100 million it got for the promotion of the arts-through the National Gallery and the National Museum among other agencies-got the former Liberal administration into trouble.
It was knocked publicly on the basis that it amounted to a $100 gift for the eggheads at a time when the old age pensioners were being given a stingy $6 increase.
Dr. Albert Trueman who was appointed to run it, didn't help. He had a built-in reputation for extravagance and disregard of the tax dollar that did neither he, the Council or culture much good.
For he was the civil service brass hat who got his knuckles rapped, in the days he ran the National Film Board, for buying television sets at public expense for his staff.
This sort of comment is, in my view, nonsense. It is worthless, but it is the kind of criticism we can expect to find in certain quarters about the activity of an organization such as the Canada Council. I recall one man who whenever he got going on this theme used to refer to "culture vultures" or "those long-haired nut boys". It seems to me we have to keep a balance in this regard if we are in any way interested in education or the arts. We have just been talking about deficiency payments on grain. Well, the Canada Council represents the making up of a tremendous deficiency in the two fields I have just mentioned.
I would say the council is doing an excellent job. I could think of a number of criticisms, and I can think of one that is current in university circles, namely that too

I know that a good many hon. members of this house who are familiar with university residences will realize that the reading rooms, however genteel and pleasant, are not the most important part of the building. This may be an example of an area in which the Canada Council should watch its expenditure. At the same time, no one who has been around universities will fail to agree-and I know you will not, Mr. Speaker-that residence requirements are very urgent. I know that you and other hon. members have been pressing the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) in this connection.
One of the other things we must keep in mind in connection with the Canada Council is that pressure by people with political influence in so far as scholarships and grants are concerned should be kept to a minimum. One of the general observations I would make about the academic and arts communities in Canada is that they are a little bit tarred with the puffing attitude to which we have become accustomed over so many years with respect to all Canadian literary and artistic achievements. We tend to blow them up more than they really merit by world or by North American standards.
And I think this sometimes applies to the kind of references which must be forthcoming from the Canadian academic community with regard to scholarships. This is a question which must occur to anyone who looks at the format of the various scholarships. I believe that the Canada Council should ask applicants to be as factual and as bald as possible. One could possibly find, reading the list of the people who have received scholarships so far, some who did not deserve them on merit. At the same time the list is a wonderful thing to look at when one remembers that until a few years ago the people in the fields of science and engineering had so many more marvellous opportunities for scholarships, both pre-doctoral and postdoctoral. This program has been a wonderful incentive to everyone in the arts faculties in Canadian universities.
I cannot finish my comments on this without saying how pleased we were in our particular area about having our own lake-head college of arts, science and technology recognized by the council. One of the things that concerned me when the early grants were going out was that contributions were going largely to the big establishments already in existence. It appeared from the first grants that those who already had were going to get, and that the new and

The latest list of awards scotched that feeling and indicates that the Canada Council has a wide point of view, and makes it clear that the growing and hopeful universities developing in northern Ontario, in Sudbury and in North Bay, are going to get a certain amount of help from Canada Council grants.
Perhaps this may destroy the validity of some of my early remarks about people in politics not pressuring, but there is one particular topic I should like to see supported by the Canada Council. Nevertheless, I think this project should be dear to the hearts of all members of parliament because it relates to the collection of information which is of particular usefulness as far as parliamentary speeches are concerned. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this matter. I believe it is an important question but our position may be expressed in a few words. It would be most difficult if all the estimates of the house were referred to committees. It would make it almost impossible to carry on and it would certainly be impossible if the committees were to sit while the house is sitting.
On behalf of this group I want to say that the sending of departmental estimates to specialized committees or to the estimates committee is a useful practice. It is of interest not only to hon. members of these committees but to the public in general whom they represent if on periodic occasions at least certain departmental estimates are referred to a committee for particularized study. A committee calls before it officials of the department concerned and hon. members are able to conduct an interrogation and obtain information and answers it would be impossible to obtain on the floor of the house.
As far as this group is concerned as long as not too many estimates are referred at one time and as long as committees do not sit when the house is sitting we would say that judging even from the brief experience last year this is a good principle and should be continued. Fisheries are of vast importance

Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful for the support given to this motion by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) on behalf of his group. I cannot quite understand the attitude being taken again today by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). I think he will agree that in years past the committees have not been given sufficient work to do and that in many cases the estimates of the departments could have been considered by a committee much more effectively than is possible when the house is in committee. Let us remember that these estimates always come back from the standing committees to the committee of the whole house.
Some years ago a start was made in having a standing committee consider estimates when the committee on external affairs was set up. As I have said on numerous occasions when discussing this subject in the house, that external affairs committee from the very beginning has done excellent work. speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REFERENCE OF SUBJECT OF HUMANE SLAUGHTER TO COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
That the subject of humane slaughter of food animals be referred to the standing committee on agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate, as I know the house will, that it is now some time since the government first undertook to introduce legislation which will ensure that food animals in Canada are killed by humane methods. The fact is that it has been a most difficult and complicated problem to devise legislation which would be effective and at the same time be fair and workable. I should like to give the house a brief history of the efforts we have made to accomplish this objective.
This government from the outset has accepted the necessity of additional legislation to ensure that humane methods are used in the slaughter of animals in Canada. This in itself marks an important step forward, for the fact is that our predecessors never accepted this position, or if they did they refused to consider that it was necessary or possible for such legislation to be introduced by the dominion government. There is as a matter of fact quite a lengthy history of discussion of the problem in the House of Commons and elsewhere, a history of efforts being made by members of the Conservative party when in opposition, on their own behalf and in support of the position taken by humane societies, to persuade the former government to take action and of the refusal of that government to do so. However, I shall not go into the details of the earlier controversy but will confine myself to an outline of the steps taken since we assumed responsibility and undertook to introduce legislation to carry out our policy in this field.
It is interesting and significant to note that since we have first begun to move in this connection the idea of legislation has not been opposed by the main spokesmen for the meat packing industry. In fact, their representatives on the meat packers council of Canada have at all times in their discussion with us agreed that legislation in this field is necessary and desirable. They have never opposed our efforts to find a practical legislative formula; their concern has been to find a suitable and fair scheme of legislation. They have co-operated with us throughout in working to this end.
At this point I should express the very real appreciation of myself and my colleagues in the government for the work done and the help we have received from all those who have been involved in this problem. I refer
Humane Slaughter of Livestock especially to the initiative shown by the various humane societies across Canada and their individual representatives; also to the co-operation of the meat packers council of Canada and the very extensive research that they have carried on. In general, although there has been some conflict and differences in points of view between those two organizations they have worked with a good deal of co-operation and harmony to achieve the desired end.
I should also express our appreciation to the officials of the department of my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, who for a number of years now has maintained a close and active liaison with the other organizations engaged in research in this field and also carried on extensive research on their own to develop humane killing methods which would be practical and applicable to the Canadian industry. I should mention also the work of the officials of my own department who have laboured long and earnestly, as the members of this house know, to devise legislation which will meet the problem. Finally, I should express thanks to our own members of parliament who, throughout the past two years, have given the benefit of their study and advice.
Our first approach to the problem was to seek an answer through the medium of the Criminal Code. There is already a general provision in the code regarding cruelty to animals, and inasmuch as the criminal law is within dominion jurisdiction, it seemed to us a logical approach to seek an answer by way of amendment to that provision.
A bill was accordingly drafted by my department during the first session after the election of 1957. This bill was introduced on December 21 of that year as Bill No. 241, and was given first reading on that date. In a statement reported at page 2713 of Hansard I outlined the government's approach and intention, emphasizing that the object in introducing the bill and giving it first reading only was to make it available to the house and the country for study. I stated that we recognized that this is a difficult and complicated problem, and that we hoped to receive the advice of all those concerned, including especially the provincial attorneys general who would be responsible for enforcement of the proposed law, with a view to studying their comments and removing any defects or weaknesses that might be shown to exist before reintroducing the legislation at a subsequent session.
As an indication of the government's approach to the problem that had to be solved, I should refer to the following quotation from that statement:
There is, then, general agreement that humane methods of slaughter exist and can be made

Humane Slaughter of Livestock applicable in Canada although there are still some problems to be solved. In considering our course of action we have had to bear the following factors in mind. First, that there is a measure of divided responsibility, and that in any criminal legislation to be introduced we must bear in mind that the responsibility for enforcement rests with the provinces. Second, that hasty action on the part of the government might force out of business abattoirs and packing plants and could result in a shortage of such commodities as bacon, etc. Third, that impracticable or unenforceable legislation does more harm than good. Fourth, that the provinces have an interest in the matter especially from the point of view of enforcement, and therefore should be consulted.
Following the introduction of that bill, and its distribution by us to various interested organizations and officials, we did receive some comments. These came mainly from the attorneys general of the provinces, six of whom replied to our letter. To be quite frank about it, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the attorneys general greeted the draft bill with something less than enthusiasm. The general effect of their comments was to question whether the bill as drafted was really sound criminal legislation, and two or three of them raised very serious questions about the problem that would arise with regard to its enforceability. We also received replies from some of the humane societies and others, these replies being generally favourable to the proposal.
We accordingly studied the matter further to give effect so far as we could to the observations that we had received. I must admit that in view of the criticisms that had been made we had some reservations about the course being followed, but after we had worked further over the bill in our department we felt that we had made a substantial step toward removing the objections, and accordingly introduced a further bill in the session following the election last year. This bill proceeded on the same basis as the earlier draft, namely by way of an amendment to the Criminal Code, and was given first reading as Bill C-32 on June 25, 1958.
I should tell the house now that we had been somewhat surprised that we had received relatively few comments and suggestions after the original bill had been introduced and made available for distribution. The fact is that it was only after Bill C-32 was introduced in June of last year that we began to receive some of the representations and suggestions we had hoped to receive earlier and which we had invited. These representations now came from a wide variety of sources and indicated a very real and legitimate concern about the effects of the new proposed legislation. Meetings were at once arranged with all those who indicated a desire to meet with us and very full discussions were held

in an effort to assess the exact nature of the problems raised in each case and the merits of the criticisms or suggestions advanced. Following these meetings, we made a further study of each proposal in an effort to see if we could amend the legislation to meet those points which we found to be substantial.
I will not take the time of the house at this stage to particularize all the criticisms and suggestions we received or the efforts we made to meet them. It will be enough to say that a number of them seemed to be substantial and legitimate. For a more detailed discussion of the situation in which we then found ourselves I would refer the house to my statement made on September 6, 1958, reported at page 4705 of Hansard for that date.
In essence, we found that in order to ensure the realization of our objective by way of legislation under the Criminal Code, and yet meet all the legitimate objections and criticisms which had now been raised, we would have to particularize to such an extent that it was doubtful whether the final result would be sound criminal legislation. We were driven to the conclusion that what would emerge would amount almost to a form of regulation rather than legislation, and it became very doubtful whether such a form of enactment would stand up as valid criminal law.
At this point, I should make it clear that the objections we received at that stage were not, as has sometimes been suggested, made by large packing concerns, but came in the main from some small individual packers, from religious organizations concerned with the question of ritual slaughter, and from individual farmers and farm organizations. In the result, we came to the conclusion as I advised the house at that time, that it was not possible within the time at our disposal before the end of the last session, to find a legislative formula which would resolve all the objections which had been brought to our attention. I, accordingly, advised the house that it was not our intention to proceed with Bill C-32 at that session, but to study the matter further and then refer the whole question at this session, together with the government's suggestions, to an appropriate committee of the house. As I then said:
It is my hope that in the meantime all concerned will give the matter further consideration and prepare their submissions, so that at an early date next session the committee may proceed with its study and hear evidence which should be helpful in enabling parliament to determine the best course to follow in bringing about a solution.
It may be helpful to the house and to the committee if at this point I summarize the

objections which we had received and which we felt raised points of substance, and which indeed led us to question whether it was possible to find a satisfactory answer by way of criminal legislation. The main objections are as follows:
1.	The best provision that could be devised for the Criminal Code failed to meet the legitimate demands of almost every interested group. This is illustrated by the following paragraph from my statement of September 6, 1958, which appears at page 4705 of Hansard:
The submissions which raised new considerations deal with such points as the problem of providing for those cases where slaughter, or preparation for slaughter, is carried out in conformity with certain religious ritual; the designation of approved appliances; the availability in Canada of equipment necessary particularly in the case of certain classes of animals; the desirability of defining 'humane method' in advance so those installing certain devices will know for certain that the expenditures made will not be thrown away; the problem of legislating in such a way that large commercial slaughterhouses will be covered without at the same time imposing conditions which it is impracticable or impossible for small concerns or individual farmers to comply with, all matters which present real problems when criminal legislation is concerned.
2.	Any provision prepared for the Criminal Code in an attempt to meet all or most of these points would have to be so limited or hedged about with qualifications that there must be some doubt that it is a valid criminal law.
3.	A Criminal Code provision must yet contain some such general expressions-such as humane slaughter-that it will be given different meanings in different parts of Canada, and even by different magistrates in the same general localities.
4.	It cannot be expected that local police authorities could obtain anything like 100 per cent compliance with such a provision in the Criminal Code. Enforcement would call for a specialized type of enforcement officer who would not be available to most of the police forces, and it was indicated to us that, in any event, more pressing problems of criminal law enforcement would, as far as our police forces are concerned, take priority over the inspection of packing houses.
5. A Criminal Code provision might force out of business many smaller plants who found that they could not afford the expensive type of installation which would undoubtedly be used by the larger plants and who, finding themselves unable to afford these sure-fire methods, would not be prepared to run the risk of using some other method and thus the risk of being branded as criminals. Such a development would
10, 1959	1789
Humane Slaughter of Livestock have the effect of further concentrating the meat packing business in the hands of a few large organizations.
6.	The attempt to particularize in order to meet legitimate objections would have the effect of turning the bill into a form of regulation rather than legislation and thus into one of doubtful validity as criminal law. On the other hand, or on the other side of the picture, if we merely enact a Criminal Code provision of broad general application in order to meet that objection, this would have the effect of extending its scope to such an extent as to make potential criminals out of farmers who kill animals on their own farm for their own consumption, for which purpose it is obviously not sensible to require the installation of expensive slaughter devices.
In the face of these formidable difficulties we sought an alternative approach which would not be open to this type of objection. We accordingly turned our attention back to a consideration of the Meat and Canned Foods Act which we had previously considered but had rejected in favour of the approach by way of the Criminal Code. That act provides for inspection of all animals intended for slaughter in any establishment as defined in the act, and also authorizes the governor in council to make regulations for the carrying out of the provisions of the act. In view of the difficulties we had encountered under the Criminal Code approach, we came to the conclusion that a satisfactory alternative might well be found by way of amendment to the Meat and Canned Foods Act which would establish, or give power to establish, the conditions and methods by which slaughter must be carried on in any establishment in order for it to conform to the requirements of the legislation.
I should point out that when we had considered this possibility previously it had been rejected on the grounds that there was at that time no agreement as to whether specific humane killing devices then being considered would in fact be effective or feasible for use in commercial operations. In view of this disagreement and uncertainty at that time it did not seem wise to contemplate making regulations requiring the use of specific devices about whose suitability there was such widespread question.
Since then, however, there has been a great deal of further active research. New devices have been discovered, and devices already in existence have been modified and perfected, particularly in the case of electrical stunning machinery. As a result of our latest discussions with experts in this field, we now
1790	HOUSE OF
Humane Slaughter of Livestock believe that it is practicable to make regulations which can be adapted to different types and sizes of operation, and yet ensure that in each case a properly supervised and workable method of humane killing will be installed.
There are, it is true, advantages and disadvantages to both approaches. In view of the advances and discoveries which have recently been made, however, the approach how being discussed by way of amendment to the Meat and Canned Foods Act seems to be the most feasible one. The main considerations in its favour are as follows.
1.	Since it is obvious that what is needed is regulation and supervision, action under the Meat and Canned Foods Act, which in its very essence is an inspection regulation scheme, will accomplish the objective most readily without any question of jurisdiction or validity of that legislation.
2.	The regulation under such an inspection scheme will be effective, uniform and scientific, and enforcement will also be uniform and effective, because enforcement will be under the supervision of one authority instead of widely diversified authorities with different interpretations resulting in confusion and hardship to a legitimate industry. Trained inspectors will be available for the purpose.
3.	Under such a proposal, the necessary detailed regulations can be made which will permit the ensuring of the over-all objective while at the same time adapting the requirements to the circumstances and needs of individual operators. Without relaxing the overall standard-namely that killing must be by a humane method-nevertheless there can be variation, under an effective scheme of supervision, as between different sizes and types of operation. Thus the absence of the element of rigidity necessary in criminal legislation will avoid making criminals out of those who have no criminal intent.
4.	This new approach should remove the objections which have been made by so many under the other approach, especially the objections of law enforcement officers, and thus should ensure that the objective is achieved with the co-operation of all concerned instead of arousing potential hostility and criticism from provincial authorities and farm organizations.
In the foregoing, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to summarize for the house the salient features of both these proposals which the government has so far worked out. From what I have said, I think it will be obvious that our view at present is that the second proposal is the best and most practicable way of achieving the objective upon which, I am sure, all are agreed. But the main purpose of this resolution is to enable a committee


of the House of Commons to study the whole question and to decide for itself what course it thinks is the best one to follow. It is the view of the government that in a matter of this kind we should not take rigid positions, and that the members of all parties should have an opportunity to hear and consider all the suggestions that may be advanced as to how the problem should be solved.
The government proposes therefore to make available to the committee, if this resolution carries, two draft bills, one embodying each of the proposals that we have so far had under study. The government will welcome the assistance of the committee in perfecting either of these proposals or, if the committee wishes, in working out and recommending any new legislative scheme which commends itself to the committee.
By referring this subject in this way to the standing committee on agriculture, the house will ensure that the fullest and freest inquiry is made to enable members to arrive at a determination of this problem. I should remind hon. members of the terms of reference of the standing committee, as found at page 803 of Hansard for February 9 of this session. By the usual routine motion made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) immediately the committees were constituted, this house provided:
That the standing committees of this house be severally empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may be referred to them by the house, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records.
If the resolution is adopted the committee would be enabled immediately to commence its inquiries and to call before it representatives of such interested bodies as may wish to come or the committee may wish to hear and whom the committee considers qualified and able to assist it in its study. The government of course will be only too glad to co-operate with the committee in making available officials from the Department of Agriculture and my own department, or any others who may be desired, to assist and advise. Since the committee is empowered to report from time to time its opinions and recommendations it will be possible for the committee to recommend which course it thinks most suitable or, if it wishes, to suggest some alternative proposal. It is our hope that the committee will commence this important work without delay. There are, I know, several organizations who are prepared as soon as they receive word to appear before the committee.
Mr. Speaker, the government regrets, as I know all members of the house do, that the difficult and complicated nature of this

problem has so far prevented a final solution. But I believe we are entitled to take some credit for the efforts that have been made so far; it is also fair to say that as a result of these efforts, and as a result of the readiness of this government to look for and implement an acceptable course of action, we are now very near a final solution. If this resolution passes, as I trust it will, then with the help of the committee to whom this subject is now being referred we expect and intend to bring in legislation at this session.

I think everybody would agree that that principle should be incorporated in our legislation. However, I cannot feel very proud of the fact that we, as Canadians, are so insensitive and callous about animals that this kind of legislation is necessary. Surely it does not reflect very much credit on our attitude toward animals if such a thing is so widespread that it can be dealt with only in this way. Speaking personally, I think this legislation, while it may afford some sort of answer, is certainly not the best answer. Education is perhaps a better answer.
The hon. minister has referred to weaknesses in legislation in dealing with this type of problem. Perhaps the main weakness is that having once passed this legislation in this house we will be able to rest our consciences and say that we have done our job. But the end result is what is important. Even if we do pass a bill setting forth certain requirements with regard to humane slaughtering, unless it produces that result we are not any better off. What result is produced by any legislation which we pass in this respect depends, as the hon. minister himself said, upon the provincial authorities, because it is they who are going to enforce this legislation.
One of the things which has caused me concern since I came to the House of Commons is that we have put a great many bills and laws on the statute books and then washed our hands of them because we cannot do anything about them. Certainly if this subject does concern us so much, we should, if we are in earnest about it and want to come to grips with the problem, try to work out some sort of understanding with all the provinces concerned so that we would have their assurance that they, in turn, would make an earnest effort to enforce this legislation to produce the result we want. The fact that the hon. minister mentioned that some of the provincial attorneys general were not too enthusiastic about it does not reassure us that they will make a very great effort to enforce any bill we may pass in this house concerning this problem.
When we deal with the subject of humane slaughtering we are at once up against the fact that it is a very controversial subject. Different peoples and organizations have very different ideas as to what is humane and what is not humane. I do not know how the committee can prevent itself from getting into a sort of academic excursion on this kind of thing. At best, I suppose we can collect all sorts of opinions, but how are we going to get worthwhile scientific advice that a certain course is more humane than another? I was glad that the hon. minister said that the second draft made provision to take care of slaughtering under different situations. For

I think we all heartily agree with that approach. I think I understand perfectly what the hon. minister says, but I still do not know how he can be so sure that each method is humane to the same degree. I would think that would depend upon scientific research and knowledge, which I doubt whether the committee would be in a position to assess.
The motion itself refers only to animals slaughtered for food. But if we are in agreement on the principle of humane slaughter of animals, why should it be confined only to animals slaughtered for food? The principle should extend to all animals. Perhaps the minister will tell us he is confining this measure to animals killed for food because these are the only ones which can be given effective protection. But certainly the principle is the same, and we cannot say it is a crime to slaughter animals intended for food in a particular way but that it is not a crime to slaughter other animals in the same way.
Along the coast of Newfoundland we have the seal hunt, and a great deal of concern has been expressed about the methods employed in the killing of seals. These methods have been handed down for generations; they have been born out of practice and perhaps it would not be easy to change them without upsetting the industry. These animals are not


taken for food but I think the same principle should apply to them as applies to other animals. I cannot see any logical reason in why a cow, for example, must be slaughtered humanely and why a seal need not be. In addition, of course, there are animals which are slaughtered in laboratories and in colleges for the purpose of research. Animals are also slaughtered in civic institutions which pick up stray cats and dogs and put them to death. Should we not be interested in their fate, too? Why should we confine our interests only to animals we are going to eat, such as cows, pigs and sheep.
To my mind, the principle is important. If we are going to adopt it, and if we really believe in it, let us not limit its application but try to extend it as far as humanly possible. No doubt all these matters will receive due consideration when the whole question goes before the committee.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF SUBJECT OF HUMANE SLAUGHTER TO COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our group is most interested in the motion which is now before the house. I may also say I followed with close attention the closing remarks of the previous speaker because I have for a long time been interested in the entire field of legislation concerning the killing not only of animals but of birds; not only in the destruction of seals but also in the trapping of animals to provide furs for beautiful women and of birds to provide feathers for the use of beautiful women. It is a very broad and interesting subject.
However, this afternoon I wish to confine my remarks to the specific subject matter before us in resolution No. 11. We in this group support the motion. Having heard the remarks made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), I am able to say that fully and emphatically. We did have a few doubts on the basis of the wording of the motion itself. However, we remembered the interest taken by the minister in this subject of recent years. We remember Bill No. 241 introduced in December of 1957 and also Bill C-32 introduced in June of 1958 and the very definite statements made by the minister that specific action would be taken this session after interested organizations and individuals had had an opportunity to study the bill and its wider context. But we were a little disturbed when we saw in the motion provision merely for the reference of the subject matter to the committee on agriculture. We wondered just what was going on. However, now that we have the assurance of the minister that two draft bills will be placed before the committee on agriculture, we feel a great deal more content. As a matter of fact, we now look forward with a great deal of confidence

to something being done this session, in view of the minister's statement that as far as he is concerned it is the intention to have a bill introduced before the recess if he is able to get the report back in time.
As the previous speaker has pointed out, this is undoubtedly a matter on which there has been some controversy, though not on the question of principle involved. Certainly there could not be any controversy with regard to the principle of the humane slaughter of animals. I noted the remarks made by the minister when he began his statement commending certain organizations for the interest they had taken in this matter.
I should like to add one group to this list -one which I believe he left out inadvertently. I refer to the employees in the packing industry. These are the people who have to do the actual slaughtering and year after year, at conventions of the united packing house workers union, they have asked for legislation which would make humane slaughter of animals compulsory. When one looks at the subject from the point of view of these workers one can really understand the necessity for enacting such legislation. It is true that in this past year some of the packing houses have been making changes but formerly, at any rate, any hon. members who have gone through packing houses would have found animals being killed with sledge hammers. If the hammer hits right, the animal is stunned and that is it. But when you have a restive animal, or an animal with an unusually thick skull, if the hammer just does not hit right the animal does not lose consciousness and one must consider not only the terrible pain suffered by the animal but also the harmful reaction on the human being who has to wield the sledge hammer and who has to go back on the floor to try to knock the animal unconscious. After the sledge hammer, they use what is known as a shackling chain or a logging chain by means of which the animal is hoisted up. Sometimes the chain slips or breaks and the animal falls down from a considerable height on to the floor. It is understandable why the employees are so insistent and unanimous for the need of some changes being brought about.
I know the interest which the Minister of Justice has taken in this matter and I am not suggesting that there has been any stalling, but may I say that I never understand why this country, which maintains that it is so progressive, should be so many years behind the United Kingdom, Denmark and the Scandinavian countries which have been using methods of humane slaughter for many years.
10, 1959
Humane Slaughter of Livestock
As to referring this question to a committee for further study, I do admit to some doubt as to whether a committee would be in better position to decide which are the best methods of humane slaughter than, for example, the Department of Justice or the Department of Agriculture or the other organizations which are concerned, on the basis of the studies which have been carried out. I am not going to go into that. If the government feels a doubt but knows something has to be done concerning the problem what better procedure could be followed than to refer it to a committee of members of parliament from all parties? That is a basically good principle.
From my own reading and because of my personal interest in this matter I have learned that there are not less than three practical methods for the slaughter of animals. I shall not take up the time of the house in discussing these because this will be a question for the committee. However, I submit that if it is not already the intention, the Minister of Justice or the Department of Agriculture should prepare a factual, scientific presentation concerning the methods of humane slaughtering. As I said, there are three methods. There is what is known as the captive bolt pistol and concussion stunner, the carbon dioxide method and the one mentioned by the minister, the electrical stunner method.
I would like the assurance of the minister that a scientific brief on each of these methods will be immediately prepared for use by the committee setting out any objections that may exist to any of these methods. I have never heard any objections to the first or second methods I mentioned but I understand there is some slight objection to the electrical stunner method because unless the bleeding knife is used very quickly there can be a certain degree of blood coagulation which is not good with respect to certain types of meat when it goes on the retail counter. However, these are matters that undoubtedly will be considered.
At this time I should like to ask an indirect question which I know the minister will answer later. I am interested in knowing what is the interpretation of the words, "the humane slaughter of food animals." I take it that this would include poultry. Millions of fowl are killed for food in Canada each year. There are three methods in current use for the killing of fowl. You may wring their necks, cut off their heads or use an instrument that has many names but which I have frequently heard referred to as an ice pick knife. The latter is reputed to be the most humane method of their slaughter.

Humane Slaughter of Livestock
I understand that in Europe and in many parts of the United States a sure-fire method of the humane killing of fowl is used. I refer to the electric knife. I am wondering whether the humane slaughter of poultry will be included in the terms of reference of this question? We in this group feel it should be included.
There was one matter on which the minister did not enlarge. Perhaps I can understand why because it is highly controversial and delicate matter for discussion. However, it is not a question we can avoid. I was hoping to hear more from the minister concerning ritual slaughter. I appreciate that it presents a problem but it is a question we cannot ignore. This is a matter upon which there must be a clear understanding.
I personally do not wish to see action taken that would hurt the beliefs of any religious group with respect to their ritual but at the same time I cannot conceive of a religious group, no matter what it is, objecting to some form of humane slaughter. I know that last year this raised a problem in the mind of the minister. I do not have the record here but if I recall correctly the minister explained last year that the question of ritual slaughter represented one reason why the matter will be delayed for further study. I sincerely hope that in the interval an answer has been found that will not interfere with the religious beliefs of any group with respect to dietary practice and that will ensure the humane slaughter of animals.
I believe I have dealt with the main points we in this group have in mind. I am in accord with the approach the minister has taken with respect to priority being given to consideration of the Meat and Canned Foods Act. It is my hope that he will have a bill to introduce at this session. We appreciate the clear exposition given to us concerning what the minister has in mind with respect to the procedure to be followed concerning the bills. We in this group are heartily in accord with this procedure and support the motion now before us.

Mr. Speaker, there are one or two comments that have been made by speakers in support of the motion which I think should be answered now in order that the answers may be on the record before the committee in so far as the intention of the government is concerned. Of course, the committee is the master of its own procedure but to the extent that it may be of assistance in terms of guidance to the

committee it may be useful to have this information on the record.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) referred to the difficulty-the sort of moral problem-we have here in enacting legislation in parliament and then perhaps being tempted to sit back and say, "we have now put the legislation on the statute books and so we have done everything that is necessary." As he said, we so often leave it to the provincial authorities to enforce these laws. That indeed was one of the weaknesses of the Criminal Code approach and it is one of the reasons why we felt that a more sound approach-once some other problems had been solved-would be by regulation under the Meat and Canned Foods Act because if it is done by regulation under that act then the enforcement will be a dominion responsibility and the same authority that has passed the legislation will have the moral responsibility of enforcing it thereafter.
The hon. member also mentioned the problem-the moral problem again, if you like,- of passing legislation to deal with one category of animals, namely food animals, and leaving out some others. He referred specifically to the question of municipal pounds and the municipal authorities who round up stray animals and have them destroyed. The only answer I can give to that question is that we can only take action and deal with those things over which we have jurisdiction and control. Where particular municipal authorities provide by bylaw for the destruction of stray or injured animals, I would think that it was no great problem at all for the municipal voters concerned to ensure that the municipal authorities will also see to it that slaughter is done by humane methods.
The same general remarks might be made with respect to one aspect of the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I can assure the hon. member for Vancouver East that it is our intention to make our officials, both in my department and in the Department of Agriculture, available to give the fullest evidence, help and advice, if asked for, to the committee both with regard to the legal problems and the implications of those problems and with regard to scientific and technical aspects of humane killing devices. The Department of Agriculture particularly has one or two, if not more, that I know personally, very highly qualified experts who have done a great deal of research in this field, whose evidence would I think be very valuable to that committee.
The hon. gentleman also asked whether the use of words "food animals" in the terms of reference was sufficiently inclusive to permit

of the committee inquiring into the humane killing of poultry. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker,
I prefer the words "humane killing" to the words "humane slaughter" because it seems to me to be a contradiction in terms. I think the words "humane killing", while not altogether void of some contradictory aspects, are more logical and fitting to use.
In the draft bill we first introduced under the Criminal Code it is true that poultry were not defined as food animals, the reason being at that time we were informed that there has been no agreement that a device has yet been developed which was capable of application to the poultry killing industry all across Canada. I understand now-this is confirmed by what the hon. gentleman himself has said-there have been improvements made in the methods of killing poultry and, certainly in so far as the terms of reference are concerned, it would be my view that the term "food animals" is wide enough to include poultry. I can see no reason for suggesting that there should be any limitation if the committee wants to look into that. Again, the committee is master of its own procedure. If it wishes to discuss poultry under these terms of reference there would be no reason why it should not.
Lastly, with respect to the matter of ritual slaughter, I recognize fully it is a problem on which I think the committee will want to receive evidence. The problem there is not so much in the slaughter itself, the actual killing of the animal, as it is in the steps which must be taken in preparing the animal for the stroke of the knife. I am informed that, properly carried out, this method of killing the animal is as humane as any method yet devised. The stroke of the knife produces instant unconsciousness, but the problem in large packing plants is to find a method of controlling the animal so that it can be held steady for that scientific stroke of the knife. Frankly, under the Criminal Code approach we found that we either had to make a blanket exception of ritual slaughter, in which case we were told the inference drawn by those concerned was that we were branding their method of slaughter as cruel, -they said, "It is not cruel at all"-or else go into such detail in the proposed enactment that it would not have been criminal law at all; it would have been the purest and simplest regulation and a regulation which, as I said before, was not sound criminal law. It was one of the main reasons why we felt we should go back and have another look at the other approach. Under the other approach it was suggested that we could make detailed regulations which are valid, sound and enforceable as to steps

Therefore, from that point of view alone it seemed to us that the new approach was much the soundest way to deal with the problem.
The committee will certainly have evidence on that subject before it as well as on all others which will enable it to make up its mind as to what is the best form of legislation to report back to the house.

AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-16, to amend the Canada Elections Act (absentee voting).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill, as indicated on the order paper, is to
[The Deputy Chairman.]
so amend our elections act as to allow for a system of voting called absentee voting. Perhaps I should explain that there is confusion sometimes in the minds of some people as between a system of absentee voting and the system of advance polls. The advance polls are special polling days, the Thursday, Friday and Saturday of the week preceding election day, upon which only certain selected classes of people may vote. The absentee system of voting is such as to allow an elector, on the normal election day, to vote at a polling station other than the one in which he is registered. It is an attempt to ensure, to the broadest possible extent, that the right of citizens to vote and the opportunity of citizens to vote at elections are guaranteed.
This bill, while it certainly may not be complete in all details, is as complete as it possibly can be, having in mind our present act. It was patterned after the system of absentee balloting now in effect in the provinces of British Columbia and Saskatchewan. In addition to that, it was drafted in consultation with the very capable law officers of the crown. Not only do we have this system of allowing people to vote if they are absent from their home town on election day in British Columbia and Saskatchewan, but there is something akin to it in the province of Ontario. However, in Ontario the provision is confined to one group of people, namely mariners. This is a system of proxy voting whereby a mariner who is absent may authorize a relative to cast a vote for him.
This bill envisages two types of ballot: one, the ordinary ballot to which we have all been accustomed with the names of the candidates printed thereon, and the other a special ballot paper which would be used by people who were absent from the constituency within which they are registered. This would be a blank ballot in order that the name of the candidate for whom the person wishes to vote may be printed in the blank space or blank spaces if there are multi-member constituencies involved.
There has been a considerable amount of discussion in past years about this, and in every session objections have been raised to the effect that it would be almost impossible to institute such a system as would extend from British Columbia to Newfoundland. The objection concerns the time involved when a person registered in British Columbia happened to be in Newfoundland on election day, and that ballot cast in Newfoundland has to be returned to British Columbia. In an attempt to overcome that difficulty this time the absentee voting is to be confined to the province within which a person is registered or to an adjacent province. In this way, three provinces

could be covered by the absentee balloting provision. An attempt is made also to lengthen the period of time between nomination day and election day. At the moment the act provides for a nomination day 28 days before the election day for ridings in the northern part of Canada in which the people are scattered far and wide. This applies to the riding I represent. The majority of constituencies in Canada have their nomination day 14 days before election day. This bill seeks to make the 28-day period between nomination day and election day universally applicable.
The purpose of this provision is to allow a sufficient length of time to prepare the ballots and get them out to all parts of Canada, that is the special and ordinary ballots. It would also allow the chief electoral officer to compile a list of candidates running in each constituency in the adjoining provinces so that each deputy returning officer, on election day, would have a list of the candidates running in each electoral district from which the absentee voter would be able to vote.
There are many hundreds of people in Canada who are now denied the opportunity to vote on election day because there is no such absentee balloting system in effect. They are denied this opportunity through no fault of their own. These people find it necessary, for business or other reasons, to be away from their home town or away from their home province on election day. I can think of a number of categories of people who find themselves in this situation. I would refer particularly to loggers who, because of the weather or because of their natural desire to get home, may find themselves either working or at some logging camp that is not in the same constituency as the one in which they were registered when the election was called. Fishermen are in somewhat the same position.
Many fishermen are not now able to fall within the provisions provided for them on advance poll voting, especially when they are some distance from the mainland and when they are away from their home town and when they operate out of camps and so on such as we do on the west coast. The advance poll system is not of too much benefit to them. The absentee system of balloting would afford them an opportunity to cast their ballot in the way that many others of us have the right to do. Our construction workers likewise move from one project to another, often times working for the same company. For some reason or another they are transferred to a different construction project and find themselves unable to cast their ballots. This absentee system would afford them that opportunity. Transport employees are in somewhat the 66968-9-114
Canada Elections Act
same category as are fishermen. Provision is there for advance poll voting but many of them do not find themselves at home within the three days which are allowed for advance poll voting.
Lawyers are another group of people who would be affected. On the day after the election in June, while I would not say I was accosted, I was speaking on the street with a good friend of mine who is a lawyer. I may say that I have a friend who is a lawyer. He was upset because he had been denied the right to vote because he had been away from his home town on a case. He was obliged to go to a sitting of the county court on election day. He had to go to some city, at any rate-I think it was of the county court-and he could not cast his ballot. Under this system he would be able to do so. Then travelling salesmen might be mentioned.
The list could be almost as long as your arm of people who, because of the category of work they have, because of demands on their time, because of the necessity of moving or travelling, find that they are not able to ballot. Candidates are in somewhat the same position, although there is some provision for them. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), for instance, in his crosscountry tour at election time could easily find himself away from his home constituency. I do not know whether that is Prince Albert or Ottawa. Whatever it is, however, he could very easily find himself away from it and not be able to cast his ballot for the candidate of his choice, whoever that might happen to be. The other cabinet ministers could certainly find themselves in the same position.
In recent years there has been some talk about cutting down the period of time for campaign purposes by reducing the number of days between the calling of the election or the issuance of the writ of election and election day itself. Those who believe that this is necessary, or believe that it should be done, believe that with the improvements in the mediums of communication and such we do not need a two month or three month period for election campaigns. They are also of the opinion that in order to cut down the time of holding elections we should have a system of permanent registration of voters. We have that system in some provinces. While a permanent voters' list is not provided for in this particular bill, nevertheless I think it is an integral part of establishing a system of absentee balloting, although it is not absolutely necessary. But if we are going to curtail the period of time for election purposes, we may find the result

Canada Elections Act
to be as has happened in the province of British Columbia where we did curtail that time. We found that the period for registration of voters is also curtailed and that people's opportunity of even getting on the voters' list is lessened much more than it is at the present time.
I am not particularly married to every word that is in this bill of which I have now moved second reading. I am concerned about the principle of ensuring to the greatest possible degree that people have the opportunity to exercise their right to ballot. As I have said, many hundreds are now denied that right for one reason or another, through no fault of their own. The speech from the throne indicated that the elections act would be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections. I for one wish that the government would hurry up and do it before this session is over so that we could start consideration of it. But, as I said earlier on another bill, if any hon. member would like to make a motion that this bill be not read a second time but that it be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections in order that they may deal with the subject matter only of the absentee ballot and report thereon to the house, I should be more than happy to accept that procedure. Does the hon. member wish to ask a question?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext: Yes; I have a question. I was wondering what effect this bill would have, if it is passed, on balloting and the final result of any given election?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I do not think it would have a great effect upon the over-all results of the election itself, unless the results of the election were close as, for instance, if we elected 125 of one party and 126 of another. On election night, with absentee balloting that could change one or two seats, we would not know the over-all results. Within the province of British Columbia we are able to know within three weeks or 21 days between election day and the final counting of the ballots.
The procedural problem is this. When a person casts an absentee ballot, he is given a ballot. He marks it and he puts it in an envelope. This is what is in effect in the province of British Columbia where we have a permanent system of registering voters. The voter signs a card when he registers. When he votes he signs his name on the front of an envelope. That envelope with the ballot in it is put in the ballot box. On election night it is opened and that particular one is then mailed to the returning officer of the constituency where the person voted and this period of time is allowed for all of these

ballots to get from each returning officer to every other returning officer. The returning officer then checks the signature on the envelope against the signature on the card. If they are the same, and it is the same voter, he opens the envelope, takes the ballot out and puts it in the ballot box. There is no violation of the secrecy of the vote, none whatever, unless only one absentee ballot was cast or unless all the voters voted for the same candidate, in which case it would not matter anyway. That happens in some instance where there is a 100 per cent ballot for one party or candidate or another.
But the time lag, as I mentioned, in one province may be longer than that, as the bill proposes, if we are to consider adjacent provinces. For instance the provinces adjacent to Quebec would be Ontario and New Brunswick. May be New Brunswick and Ontario would have a longer period of time. But with postal facilities as they are, I do not think it would be much longer than that time lag. Certainly the results would be known on election night unless the voting was fairly close so that a few votes one way or the other could alter the results. But so far as knowing the results of the election itself is concerned, we would know them on election night.
I think I have fairly well summed up the thoughts I have on the matter, Mr. Speaker. As I said earlier and as I should like to reiterate, the details of the bill are ones that I have envisaged. They are taken from our British Columbia legislation and were adapted to fit our present federal act. Has the hon. member another question?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext: I was wondering what percentages are involved. From the practical and actual experience in British Columbia, what percentage of the total vote take advantage of this opportunity?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I have not the results here with me but I can give you an idea. I cannot give you the figures province-wide because I do not think they averaged out the full number of voters in the province, but I can give you an idea in constituencies. For instance, in Skeena, the provincial riding of the same name, use of this was made by 4.7 per cent of the voters voting by absentee ballot. In another riding, that of Atlin, which is to the far north, the occupancies of many people living there take them away from their homes at election time, which is normally in June, and it is up to as high as 12 or 14 per cent. However, I may be mistaken in those figures. In an urban riding it may be relatively small, depending on the occupancies of the people. I am not concerned with every little detail set

out in the bill. What I am concerned with is giving every opportunity to people to use their absentee ballot on election day. I am sure the committee will review the elections act, and I hope it will take this matter into consideration. I think it would be extremely courteous of this house if we were to say to that committee that we would like them specifically to study this particular matter if the house does not desire to give the bill second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an involved bill and one which has as its main objective something which every member of this house will, I think, be in favour of, namely to make it possible for the voter to exercise his franchise. I know in the previous session I myself had items on the order paper dealing with advance polls, and I believe that there will be bills coming up on advance polls all with the same idea, namely to make it possible for the voter to cast his ballot for the candidate of his choice.
There are, however, in the particular bill presented to us now certain aspects of operation which should be considered. I know that the hon. member will say that they can be considered in committee; but since this is the first time that this particular bill has come before the house, I think certain consideration should be given to these various phases. For instance, in Hansard of July 4, 1956, Mr. Barnett, the former member for Comox-Alberni, when the estimates of the Secretary of State were being considered, and in particular the office of the chief electoral officer, pointed out the difficulties which the fishermen in his riding were having in that an election poll during the summer months pretty well disenfranchised them. The same is true, as the hon. member pointed out, of construction workers, lumber workers, and so on. Mr. Barnett, in speaking of this, said, as reported on page 5667 of Hansard:
Actually the only feasible way I have been able to think of for dealing with it would be by the introduction into our election act of the absentee vote. I realize there may be a great many practical difficulties in the way of the introduction of the absentee vote into our federal elections act, particularly if it were to have application across the whole country. However, I do feel it could be written into the act in a form that would apply at least within the boundaries of a given province.
Of course, Mr. Barnett was referring to the fact that in the province of British Columbia we already have such a system in use in regard to provincial elections, as the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has pointed out. However, I was interested in going back to the committee on privileges and elections for the year 1955 when the chief electoral 66968-9-1141
Canada Elections Act
officer appeared before that committee and where the very point that the hon. member has brought up was raised by various members of that committee. I do not want to quote at extreme length, but there is a statement by the chief electoral officer which bears on this particular bill. The statement starts at the bottom of page 53 of the minutes, where the chief electoral officer is attempting to tell the committee how such a system as is proposed in this bill would work. He says:
I cannot answer those questions.
They were questions by members of the committee in regard to the absentee vote.
I am not advocating that this system be adopted. I am merely explaining the mechanics it would take to provide extra facilities for electors to vote who are absent from their polling divisions in Canada or outside Canada. I am trying to explain the change which would be involved if such facilities are to be provided.
Some members of this committee have been candidates at the election with permanent lists in 1935. I think you will recall that that one experience turned out to be a failure. They had also provided absentee voting in 1935, and that experience also turned out to be a failure. At the same time this system is working out satisfactorily in other countries and I now wish to explain to the committee the mechanics involved. Taking the vote of people who are not only absent outside Canada-
The committee were there discussing people outside Canada, and that is not relevant. He goes on to say:
A permanent list requires a biennial, triennial or quadrennial revision.
That is where they have these permanent lists. These revisions are a house to house canvass. To a permanent list you attach these facilities. The first is by a postal envelope very similar to the envelope supplied to members of the Canadian forces. For people absent from their home polling division within Canada, they are supplied with a ba ot and an envelope and they write in on a ballot paper the name of the candidate for whom they wish to vote in their constituency, and that ballot is placed in the envelope and put in the ballot box.
Then the chief electoral officer went on to explain the varied safeguards which are necessary in the casting of an absentee ballot, and I am sure the hon. member for Skeena would not like to see any letting down of our guard as far as safeguards in regard to the casting of ballots is concerned. A system such as absentee balloting could lend itself to abuse if these safeguards were not present.
I believe it is not within the rules of the house that I should quote at extreme length, but the electoral officer goes on to explain the various safeguards which are necessary if a system of absentee balloting is to be used.
