Further on in the discussions of this committee, the former member for Vancouver-Burrard, Mr. MacDougall, made the statement on page 55 of the minutes that every day in the city of Vancouver for 365 days of the year there are more than 475 changes of address. He went on to point out that this would, of course, apply in a greater degree to the cities of Montreal and Toronto, and also to Winnipeg. That seems a strange statement for someone coming from Vancouver to make, because the problems of Winnipeg would, of course, be much smaller.
This system of permanent lists means a permanent register and a permanent staff. If the list is taken on a biennial basis it means it is closed as of, say, February 1. Then if an election is held on July 1, all changes between February 1 and July 1 have not been entered on the permanent list. This presents a problem, and I am not sure how it would be overcome. Hon. members know that mailing out to constituencies even now represents a major problem, and so far as I can read in the record of the committee I find no place where either the officials or the members point out how that difficulty can be overcome. As hon. members know, under our present elections act, enumeration begins 48 days before polling day and carries on for about six days. Later, the lists are published and provision is made for revision in urban ridings. In rural ridings there are no courts of revision, and anyone can vote by making an affidavit and being vouched for by another voter from the district where the person desiring to vote claims to reside. All these are checks and safeguards which have been mentioned by the chief electoral officer and which constitute perhaps the prime responsibility borne by that officer, namely to see that the election is honestly carried out. I have felt that what worried this official most throughout his evidence was

that he could not be assured as to how well these safeguards would work under a system of absentee voting.
The hon. member for Skeena has limited the problem to some degree by making his proposal applicable only to provinces adjacent to provinces where the person concerned happens to reside, but this in itself seems to be begging the question. I think that if absentee voting is the right thing to have, and if it can be carried out it should be carried out on a national basis, providing it is worth while, as it is carried out in the United Kingdom or in other nations of the commonwealth. The fact that it adds to the complexity of the situation means only that it adds to that complexity by adding to the numbers and by adding to the time which must elapse before a definite result can be brought in.
There is an old political story which may have some application here, I will not say which party it concerns. Driving through a certain province, the leader of a certain party had one of his lieutenants for that province stop his car to visit the grave of a friend who was a member of the opposite party. He turned to his lieutenant and said: this man was one of my best friends but unfortunately he did not vote the right way. And his friend said: well, he has been dead for 16 years and he has been voting for me all those 16 years. That is an old political story, but it does illustrate that we cannot be too careful in regard to the safeguards applied to ensure against fraud, and I should think that the complications added by this system of absentee voting would immeasurably complicate the task which our chief electoral officer and his returning officers have to undertake.
The suggestion that this matter should be sent to a committee for study is, I feel, unnecessary because the elections act will no doubt be discussed as a matter of course, and there will be the same type of examination as was carried out in 1955 when amendments were made to the act on the advice of the officials who are charged with the responsibility for carrying on elections. For this reason I believe that anything we say here will most likely be repeated during the hearings of the committee. All I can do is emphasize the fact that according to everything I have been able to find out in regard to absentee voting, it hinges on a permanent list. The bill might just as well have included a provision for setting up a permanent voters list, because this is the only basis upon which a scheme of absentee voting can be carried out. The setting up of such a permanent list involves further

complications; I have only referred to some of these complications in the remarks I have made.
I know this system has worked in other countries and that it has worked in at least two provinces. At least I am taking the hon. member's word that it has worked well for him as a candidate in British Columbia, and I presume, therefore, that it has worked as well for other candidates. But with regard to the constituencies of Skeena and Atlin I must say that these are vast ridings and, as the hon. member pointed out, because of the nature of the activities of the people who work in those ridings it is normal for a large proportion of the population to be unable to attend the poll on the day of an election. But this would not be true of urban ridings to anything like the same extent.

subtopic: FURTHER AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GUARANTEED LOANS ON FISHING VESSELS
speechtext:
There are one or two points I should like to mention before the resolution carries, Mr. Chairman. In the first place, I notice that the resolution states that provision will be made in the bill that a guaranteed loan may be made to a person who at one time had an interest in a fishing vessel but no longer has such an interest, or to a person who desires to acquire an interest in a fishing vessel for the first time. It will not surprise the minister if I ask him whether he has considered whether this would bar any person in Canada who may have owned a fishing vessel at any time. Does he think that there may conceivably be a conflict between this proposed legislation and the Senate and House of Commons Act?
Having asked that question, I would now go on to something about which I expect a more serious answer from the minister. As the minister is well aware, we did have a very brief debate on the original resolution regarding this bill. I regret to say I was unable to be present at that time and so was not able to say a word or two on the proposed measure. I hope the minister will bear with me if I make a few remarks that are not strictly relevant because there are some points upon which I would like him to answer at the committee stage of the bill. What I should really like to be quite sure about is

that the bill will make provision for loans to fishermen who, because of the difficulties that were experienced in certain parts of the Atlantic coast and notably in Newfoundland last year, find themselves in very straightened circumstances and who, because of the bad weather, lost part of their gear. I should like to know if the minister feels the act covers that sort of situation.
In order to illustrate my point may I cite a letter which I received just the other day from one of my constituents in Bonavista. Perhaps I could make my point more quickly by reading this letter than in any other way. The letter reads:
Dear Mr. Pickersgill:
I am writing you a note to ask if you could give me any information concerning the fishermen's losses last summer. Is there going to be any assistance for us? I lost my cod trap and all its belongings except my leader-
That does not mean "leader" in the political sense, but that is a part of the fishing gear.
-and I am not in any position to replace it. With the loss of my trap and the very bad summer you can imagine, sir, why I am asking for assistance. I wrote Captain Strickland-
That is the provincial member.
-to ask the Department of Fisheries to help me with a gift or a small loan. I am man enough to pay it back yearly if they could arrange it for me so that I could get another cod trap to fish with. It is not much good for me to write the fisheries loan board for help because I don't want an engine or a boat. I would like to get a loan to use to my own satisfaction so as to cut out credit. Charges are too high on the fishermen. Now, Mr. Pickersgill, you should remember me because I drove out to our fishing place Mifflins cove with you and Mr. Max Little last spring and it is no easy place to work, either.
He is certainly right about that.
Now, sir, do you think you could spare time to drop me a line or two telling me how I can get some help.
This is not an isolated case. Not only was there a very poor fishery, but there was a lot of very bad weather and a great many fishermen lost their gear last year. If they are not able to get some credit in some way there are a great many of these people who are just not going to have the gear necessary to earn their livelihood. If the minister feels that this would be adequately covered by the bill-I am not sure myself whether or not it would-I would appeal to him to make a special appeal to the Bank of Nova Scotia which, after all, is the principal bank so far as the outports of Newfoundland are concerned, to ask them to take special note of this situation.
I am not suggesting for a minute that the minister should urge the bank to make bad

loans. There are many of these fishermen who in a normal year would be well able to pay back the loans. They are well known as reputable people. It would be of enormous help in a very, very difficult situation.

speechtext: I have one or two comments to make, Mr. Chairman. The indicated purpose of the measure is to aid people who intend to acquire a boat or acquire an interest in a boat. I submit that the suggestion I have made is merely an extension of this selfsame principle. Here is a person who starts to build a boat. It is his intention to acquire a prescribed interest in the vessel. For one reason or another financially he is not able to complete it on his own. He then, in my opinion, should quite propertly be considered in the same light as the minister has considered the person who would be affected by this present legislation. That person should be able to go to the bank and be in the same position as anyone else would be if he fell within the scope of the provisions of the act. I think the principle is precisely the same. The individual fisherman may be just in different circumstances. One starts on his own to build a boat, or a fishing vessel as it is called, and the other does not start to build it himself but attempts to acquire it. It seems to me

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act that those two individuals should he placed on precisely the same footing so far as they are under this act.
There are a number of other matters concerning the present application of the act which are rather involved because they take into account the relationship between the native Indian as defined in the Indian Act who lives on a reserve and the banks which would make loans under this particular legislation. On the west coast, especially in the northern part from which I come, there are a great number of native Indian people and a great number of villages or reserves right on the coast line or right on the water. A great number of these native Indian people engage in fishing as their means of livelihood. Their sole means of income is through fishing. I know that this is the attitude of the bank which makes the loan to the individual and probably the bank looks at things differently than we normally would. There is a reluctance and in some instances there is a complete refusal in connection with granting loans to native Indian people who want to build their own fishing vessels and to go out and fish and to be on substantially the same footing as a nonIndian. Many of these native Indian people in years past have been able to get some sort of credit from the fishing companies, have been renting boats from fishing companies, renting their gear from them, getting credit from fishing companies for food and other provisions and at the end of the year find themselves still indebted to the fishing company for one reason or another.
A number of them that I know, particularly the Haida Indians or the Tsimshian, for some years have been engaged in fishing. Many of them want to get out of the clutches of the fishing company and want to get out and build, own and operate their own fishing vessel. They find it extremely difficult to do so under the act, as it is at the present time because of the reluctance of the banks to make loans to fishermen who are Indians. They say they have no right of recourse against the individual because he is an Indian and because he lives on a reserve. That is another matter which I think should be considered carefully by the department. I wonder whether the minister would indicate his feelings on this matter.
It would be my suggestion that inasmuch as there are a number of other thoughts about changes in the act and inasmuch as it does not apply equitably as between one person and another person because of the way in which they go about acquiring a boat or because of the colour of their skin or because of the way in which they live and so on, that these matters could very easily be dealt with in the


standing committee on marine and fisheries. While it is a matter of finance and comes under the minister's jurisdiction, nevertheless it also pertains to fishing. The committee on marine and fisheries, as a result of action taken in the house this afternoon, will be considering the estimates of the Department of Fisheries. I think we would be well advised to refer to the committee on marine and fisheries the bill that will arise out of this resolution. If the minister wants to select a banking and commerce committee because it deals with banking, that does not matter too much. However, I think the bill should go to some standing committee of the house in order that a fairly free and informal discussion may take place and that individual representations may be made to the committee with respect to additional changes in the proposed legislation. I should like to hear some comment from the minister about that particular matter.

Mr. Chairman, I want to add my voice to the pleas made by the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Like the hon. members who have just spoken, I am a little disappointed to learn that this legislation is not going to be useful as it first appeared when it was referred to in the house. Hon. members will remember that when the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg made this suggestion in debate on an earlier bill and the Minister of Finance told the house he would take it into consideration, we had great hopes that this bill would mean what it said. I had understood it was to help the person who desired to acquire an interest in a fishing vessel. If it is only going to apply to fishing vessels which are already built, or interests which are for sale, then it is not going to be of any help in my province.
What we are trying to do in Newfoundland at the present time is this. We are trying to reduce the cost of production of fish by utilizing more modern boats. These boats have to be built. Our fishermen are well able to build them themselves, and I had hoped that under this legislation they would be able to acquire a small loan which would enable them to purchase the materials required to build a vessel and equip it, thus enabling them to put to productive use their own skill and ability. We need long liners which can go offshore, say 20 to 30 miles, and come in every day. That would mean a boat costing about $10,000, equipped with a diesel engine of 60 horsepower to 70 horsepower, and a suitable amount of fishing gear. If three men could get together and get a loan under this legislation, they could very well build that boat themselves under conditions which would enable them to repay the loan without too much difficulty. At the present time the provincial legislation does not cover that particular type of boat because the provincial legislation requires specifications which are difficult to meet and which run the cost of the vessel required up to about double what the fishermen can afford to pay. If this legislation is going to be restricted by the definition of the term "fishing vessel" then the usefulness of this legislation is going to be very limited, particularly in the province of Newfoundland.
Of course, as the other hon. members have pointed out, unless the banks are prepared to make loans and take these vessels as security then this legislation is of no use at all. The success of this legislation depends first and last upon the willingness of banks to make loans. Unless they do that we might

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act just as well not pass it at all. But assuming the banks will take a favourable attitude in regard to this problem, then I think we should go as far as possible to help the fishermen make the fullest use of it.

subtopic: FURTHER AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GUARANTEED LOANS ON FISHING VESSELS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in this case it would give preference to fishermen who make application for a loan to buy a secondhand boat, and to the fisherman who wanted to acquire a new boat with an engine. 10, 1959
Public Servants Inventions Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Has the minister got an explanation?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
I might make a short explanation. This amendment is brought forward for the reasons that are given in the explanatory notes that accompany the bill. In 1954 the Public Servants Inventions Act was brought before the house and was proclaimed in 1955. At that time provision was not made for the proceeds that would come as a result of the inventions which were patented to go other than to the consolidated revenue fund. The practice has grown up over the last three years for the corporation which operates under this measure to hold these moneys and pay out the awards. The Auditor General drew attention to that, and this amendment will make regular a practice which has been followed during the last three years.
The explanatory note says that the proceeds of any patent or invention coming under the act would ordinarily go to the consolidated revenue fund. The purpose of the amendment is to permit the corporation to which the administration and control of a patent or an invention has been transferred to retain the money arising therefrom, and to require that the money be used for the purpose of this act and the purposes for which the corporation was established.
The remainder of the amendment simply makes it retroactive so that the amendment will apply to all assignments that have already been made as well as assignments that may be made in the future. This is the whole purpose of the bill which is now before the house. We are not introducing any practice that has not been followed, but are simply adding a clause to section 9 of the Public Servants Inventions Act so that the whole procedure will be in accordance with the statute.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that I am any more in favour of the Public Servants Inventions Act now than I was in 1954. I do not think that at this time I can make a speech on that subject. However, the minister has just said that the purpose of the amendment is to vest the moneys received from any invention by a public servant into a corporate agency instead of the consolidated revenue fund. This, of course, is quite true and as it should be in certain cases.
I am not at all clear, however, as to how this is done because in some cases it is true that there may be some receipts from an invention by a public servant which should be vested into a corporate agency to which they have been assigned. However, there are

Public Servants Inventions Act some cases where an invention might be assigned to a private agency. Certainly, in that case I am wondering what that corporate agency would be. I feel, therefore, that I should reserve to the committee stage my attempt to ascertain what the situation may be as contemplated by the minister. I might also restate my stand and my reasons for being against the Public Servants Inventions Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to express the support of this group for this small measure. I must say that once again we are delighted to see the government giving effect to a couple of C.C.F. principles in this minor legislation. The first one, of course, to which effect is being given is in acknowledging the value of the principle of decentralization in the administration; and the second one is in desiring to promote, apparently by this amendment, departmental initiative and the initiative of the personnel of the departments in question. In his brief statement the minister mentioned that this small amendment makes it possible for the department or the government corporation in question or agency, I presume, to retain moneys, even to the advantage of the government corporation in question. We think that is a good principle because it is, in a limited way, giving effect to the principle which I have just mentioned previously. I noted that the minister said that it was now actually giving legal effect to something which had been accepted in practice for some time. I presume it is giving legal effect to the common sense of the people who were concerned with administration as a result of experience. We support this measure wholeheartedly.

The patent laws, not so much in this country but in other countries, are very stringent. If the deputy minister should decide that he has not time to look at this invention, and it is a public servant who has invented this pencil, I will call it-and I am not interested in pencils-and he belongs to, let us say, the

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: The difficulty that arises here is that the corporation handles only the inventions that are submitted to it. In order to get the information for which my hon. friend is asking each department would have to be queried. This corporation has not that information.

speechtext: Where do they come into the act? Just in order to help the minister out may I ask this question. Have we a new corporation?

Section 9 of "An act respecting inventions by public servants" reads as follows:
9.(1) The administration and control of any invention vested in Her Majesty by this act and any patent issued with respect thereto are vested in the appropriate minister, and the appropriate minister may transfer such administration and control to any other minister or to any corporate agency of Her Majesty.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I can quite understand the hon. minister's attitude and what he has said, but surely he is not making a broad statement that all inventions submitted by public servants are referred only to this corporation?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS

Public Servants Inventions Act hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who sympathizes with the rights of ordinary people, will appreciate that in this case the section makes no sense at all, because there is no such thing as a corporate agency existing which will do this job, which is that it "shall be used for the purposes of this act and the objects and purposes for which the agency was established". Mr. Chairman, I would not mind helping the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think this is a bad section, and that is very clear to a lawyer so eminent as himself, because the section says:
Where pursuant to this section the administration and control of any invention or patent has been transferred to a corporate agency of Her Majesty, any money received by the corporate agency in the course of the administration and control of the invention or patent may be retained by that corporate agency, and shall be used for the purposes of this act and the objects and purposes for which the agency was established.

speechtext:
I appreciate fully the remarks which the hon. member has made and I appreciate fully his interest in inventors, who he thinks may not be looked after as carefully as they should be. However, under this particular bill all we are hoping to do is to add a small amendment to section 9 in accordance with the suggestion made by the comptroller general so that the moneys that are paid in may continue to go to Canadian Patents and Development Limited as they have been going for the last three years, and as they did under the former Liberal government, instead of going direct to the receiver general.
It is in accordance with that suggestion that this amendment has been put forward. The corporate agency that is mentioned here was understood by all those who were dealing with this to be Canadian Patents and Development Limited and I think perhaps that was in the mind of my hon. friend as well.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, it never was. That corporate agency is a small corporate agency of the crown as far as patents are concerned. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has some of the most important patents in this country if not in the world and this is also true of the atomic energy control board. For instance, I could also make mention of Polymer Corporation and a number of other such agencies.
I find that I am raising my voice and this is not fair. I assure the minister that I am not directing my emotional outburst against him. I would not dare raise my voice toward the Minister of Finance because we are too friendly. That hon. gentleman is a lawyer and I am sure he would say, as a lawyer, that we should put this aside for a while and do a good job of it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I point out that Canadian Patents and Development Limited has been receiving revenue from inventions which have originated with the

Public Servants Inventions Act National Research Council, the Fisheries Research Board, the Department of National Defence and the National Film Board, to mention but a few. Surely that is an indication that the system has been working satisfactorily. I have heard nothing by way of complaint, criticism or suggestion until this evening. The hon. gentleman himself has not in the past raised the problems which he is now putting before the committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: But oh, Mr. Chairman, I have. What the minister just said confirms my statement. If this is intended to place in the hands of a particular crown corporation the patents it receives the statement should be limited to that. If that is the case I would then be in a position to seek some information. I want to know a great deal about the number of patents that have been received by that particular corporation, the amount of revenue received and the plight of the inventors, et cetera. This section does not state to what corporation these matters are related.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would it make a serious difference to my hon. friend if there were several corporate agencies to which this might apply? It happens to apply to Canadian Patents and Development Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Yes, it would make a difference because it would contradict the minister's statement. He just informed us to what corporation it relates. It mentions "a" corporate agency, not "any" corporate agency. There are many questions which would follow, of course.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, apparently the hon. member is not prepared to accept my statement that we are dealing with Canadian Patents and Development Limited which is the corporation that was considered when this amendment was introduced in the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: I do not agree that it was considered at that time. I have never been at all satisfied with this act. Since registering my objections in the past this is the first opportunity I have had to find out what is happening to the inventions of public servants. I am very much surprised that my hon. friends who sit in that party to my right and who speak with such eloquence about the rights of men do not awaken and seek to find out what is happening with respect to the inventions of public servants and the benefits that accrue therefrom. Perhaps those hon. gentlemen feel we should socialize everything.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: If I may reply to that, Mr. Chairman, I would say that the hon. gentleman is confusing everyone more and more-

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Especially the hon. gentleman who is now on his feet.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: -and he is certainly confused himself. I feel that he actually misunderstood the real intent of this bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, with all the deference at my command may I suggest that the hon. gentleman completely fails to understand the meaning of this bill As a lawyer and as one who is interested in the rights of Canadian citizens I want to know what is happening to the inventions of public servants. I was very free in the criticism I made of this act under the former administration and I feel equally free to criticize this legislation now. This is a loosely drawn act that forfeits the rights of citizens perhaps simply because they are mere civil servants, as it were. As it is presently drawn any agency of the crown or any other body such as General Electric or Westing-house could take the invention of a civil servant and do what it liked with it paying only a certain royalty to be decided by the cabinet. I am sure my hon. friends would wish to see this section properly re-written.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted to ask the hon. gentleman if this bill was not passed by the former administration?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Not this bill, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: I mean the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister if this organization, Canadian Patents and Development Limited, is the organization about which we have recently read something in connection with the electronics field and the representations to Washington that became necessary on the part of the Minister of Justice? Is this the agency or entity that is involved?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Not this one, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. After all, I have not been able to get anywhere with the minister. I quite appreciate that he realizes this is a bad section and it requires amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: You said the whole bill is bad but you fellows passed it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member could assist the minister and hon. members of the committee by asking his questions in a clear, concise and systematic way in order that they may be dealt with in the same fashion?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: But surely, Mr. Chairman, I already have asked a number of questions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Yes, but not clearly.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: In the first place I want to know what is the corporate agency? I think it should be included in the bill. That is my first question. From there I am prepared to go on to ask how many patents have been sent to this agency, how many have been refused by the agency, how many people have lost their inventions because they were sent to the agency, what was the amount of revenue that accrued to the agency since its inception and what corporations have received assignments from the agency?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Put it on the order paper.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I inform hon. members opposite that they are lucky that I do not get up on my feet more frequently because as far as taking care of them verbally is concerned and meeting their silly innuendoes I am capable of doing it at any time. I am not worried about that at all. I have been pretty decent and kept to the law. We could talk in this way until 10.00 o'clock. I think the minister would agree with me that it would be much better to come around with a section that is properly drafted and also agree that somebody has drafted a bad section. It would not take much time on the next occasion to pass it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
Some of the questions which the hon. member is asking go beyond the scope of the act. He is asking about matters with regard to inventions which do not come to the attention of Canadian Patents and

Public Servants Inventions Act Development Limited. These questions can be put on the order paper and made applicable to each department, if he so desires, and he could get the answers to them. He is asking questions with regard to how many inventions have been refused by the corporation. These are things that could easily be put on the order paper and the answer could be produced and given to the hon. member at any time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
I would like to raise a point of order. We are dealing with an amendment concerning the Public Servants Inventions Act. The clause in the amending bill deals with the transfer of such inventions and patents to a corporate agency of Her Majesty. It could be any one of a great many corporate agencies of Her Majesty.
The minister is seeking to argue now that he does not have to answer questions as to the number of patents of public servants which have been granted within the time of the act, or of the inventions. Surely it is not tenable to hold such a position at all because how can the bill have any meaning if it is not to cover any of the inventions or patents of public servants, or if it is to cover part of them? What percentage is it to cover? Certainly the position is not tenable at all. Surely we are entitled to this information which is clearly within the purport of the amending bill now before the committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: I am still looking for information, Mr. Chairman. If the-minister intends to make a corporate agency I want to have a statement from him as what that corporate agency is, and whether it is the only one within the terms of the act. I am entitled to find out how many inventions have been referred to this so-called corporate agency. I know the minister is busy with my good friend, the Minister of Finance, who will soon reduce the taxes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: I hope it is not the corporation which will give the revenue. As I said before, I am entitled to get this information from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who I am sure thought that this was an innocent bill. In view of his great respect for the rights of public servants who are already under the preceding section 9, in my opinion at least, treated in a very, as the Prime Minister would say, cavalier fashion-I am not trying to imitate the Minister of Finance when I speak in this way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Go ahead, why not?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
Well, it was very successful. I ask the minister what is

Public Servants Inventions Act the corporate agency? Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce not give to the committee information as to the number of applications as distinct from patents, because these are the two things which have been referred to this agency. My second question is, what did the inventors, or the so-called inventors, get out of it and, third, which is much more important, to whom are they assigned? To what private corporations are the inventions of public servants assigned for the receipt of a very small royalty? What were the receipts and to what use were they applied?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I cannot resist getting up in view of the hon. member turning and shaking his fist at this group. We wish he would be more concerned about the human rights and fundamental freedoms of the loggers in Newfoundland and the people in Newfoundland than he is over this minor, paltry matter which is essentially for the protection of the exchequer of this country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at this time, if I were the hon. member, I would be much more concerned about the deficiency payments than the rights of the loggers of Newfoundland.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: We thought the government was worrying about that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
I would like to ask the
minister a question. He pointed out that this legislation was originally introduced by the secretary of state. At the time I happened to be the secretary of state who administered this act. How does it come about that it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce and not the Secretary of State who is sponsoring the amendment of the act?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext: At the time that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate introduced this act in 1954 he was secretary of state. He introduced it with some reluctance and in the course of that debate referred to the minister of trade and commerce to assist him. Subsequent to that it was decided by, I presume, the former government that the administration of this act might very well come under trade and commerce and that is how it happened to come to my attention.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
The minister is well aware that it is not possible to transfer the function of one department to another department
except by an order in council under the transfer of duties act. Can the minister give us the date and the number of the order in council which transferred the administration from the department of the Secretary of State to his department?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION OF MONEYS
speechtext:
I think we can get that information for the hon. member. Actually, I should have said this comes under the national research council and I happen to have some responsibility to report to parliament on behalf of the national research council. But if the hon. member wants that type of information I am quite sure that it can be given. In fact, any of the questions which have been asked tonight can be answered. There is no desire to conceal anything. Some of the information is right here. If the hon. member for Ottawa East had not taken up so much time I could have told him the people to whom the awards are being paid and the organizations from which some of those inventions have come forward and the amount of royalties which have been received, and so on, but the time has elapsed.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Tomorrow we shall commence with the bill which has just been under debate and then take item No. 6, the resolution concerning the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act; then item No. 15, the resolution concerning freight rates; then item No. 4, second reading of the act to amend the Canada Shipping Act; item No. 1, that is the act confirming an agreement between the federal government and the province of New Brunswick respecting Indian reserves, and the motion to set up the committee to study the Indian Act.

speechtext: I am not sure at the moment, but probably we would go on with estimates.
